extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy (readers of Kant); naturalists interested in philosophical methodology of teleology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts methodological maxims and evaluative principles for judging natural objects as purposes versus purely mechanical products; addresses how scientists and philosophers should balance mechanical explanation and teleological judgement when investigating organised beings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privilege of attempting mechanical explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: We should explain all products and occurrences in nature by mechanism as far as is in our power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant repeatedly emphasizes that it is 'infinitely important' not to let slip the mechanism of nature; one should 'explain all products and occurrences in nature, even the most purposive, by mechanism as far as is in our power.' Pursue comparative anatomy and mechanical principles to the limits of human understanding, because mechanistic study is indispensable for natural science and may yield empirical progress even where teleology seems to appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of teleological judgement for organised beings
rubrics_metrics.description: When an object is indubitably established as a natural purpose (an organised being), the judgement about it must be subordinated to a teleological principle because mere mechanism is inadequate for explaining its possibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that for organised beings we 'must always lay down as basis an original organisation' and that 'absolutely no human Reason ... can hope to understand the production of even a blade of grass by mere mechanical causes.' Teleology is indispensable as a heuristic and regulative principle for investigating particular laws where mechanistic explanation cannot account for purposiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology is a reflective, not a determinant, principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleological principles are only subjectively valid for our judging (reflective judgement) and do not provide determinant, objective explanations of how organised beings are produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant distinguishes reflective from determinant Judgement: teleology guides our judgement and investigation ('methodology'), but it cannot supply the a priori explanatory grounding that theoretical natural science requires. Thus one must not treat teleology as a constitutive explanatory principle that replaces mechanical derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute teleology for mechanism (nor vice versa)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not substitute teleological explanations for mechanical ones, or substitute mechanism where teleology is required; both principles have separate roles and cannot be used as constitutive explanations for the same product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant stresses that 'one method of explanation excludes the other' as determinant principles; they cannot be united in a single empirical explanation because their grounds differ. Instead, they can be related only via an indeterminate, supersensible common ground for reflective judgement. Practically: use mechanism where it suffices, and teleology where purposiveness is unavoidable, but do not conflate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination of the mechanical to the teleological in judging natural purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: In judging things as natural purposes, mechanical explanations must be subordinated to a teleological principle (i.e., treated as means under a represented purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While pursuing mechanistic investigation is 'rational, even meritorious,' Kant holds that for objects judged as natural purposes we must finally 'subordinate these grounds collectively to a teleological principle.' Mechanism can be viewed as the means by which purposive ends are realized, but the judgement of the object's possibility remains teleologically constrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teleology is methodological/regulative and belongs to the Critique of Judgement
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology does not properly belong to Natural Science or Theology as a constituent doctrine; instead, it belongs to the methodology (the Critique) for the cognitive faculty of Judgement and furnishes regulative a priori principles for judging nature by final causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues teleology 'belongs only to Criticism' and supplies the method by which nature must be judged according to final causes. Its influence on theoretical natural science is 'negative' or regulative: it guides inquiry without providing constitutive explanatory laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heuristic use of teleology (avoid transcendent/poetical explanations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teleology should be used heuristically to guide empirical investigation, but not to assert transcendent causes or to engage in poetical extravagance beyond what natural knowledge can follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant warns that appealing to a cause working according to purposes for the origination of natural forms, when taken transcendentally, becomes tautological and seduces Reason into 'poetical extravagance.' Use teleology to structure investigation but avoid claiming transcendent explanatory access to divine ideas or the mode of action of such a Being.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish internal versus external purposiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal purposiveness applies to organised beings (they are 'for' something qua organisms); external purposiveness denotes how one non-organised thing may serve as a means for another organised being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant defines external purposiveness as when things without internal purposiveness (earth, air, water) serve as means to the ends of organised beings. Only organised beings have internal purposiveness (can be asked 'what is it for?'). This distinction limits where teleological judgements are properly applied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological caution about the limits of human Understanding (supersensible ground)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparent possibility of uniting mechanism and teleology rests on a supersensible ground we cannot determinately know; thus human understanding must recognize its limits and treat such a ground as indeterminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant repeatedly notes that any principle common to both mechanical and teleological derivations must lie in the 'supersensible' and is therefore 'indeterminable' by us. Consequently, we may hypothesize the compatibility of both principles, but we must acknowledge that we cannot form a determinate explanatory concept of that ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer theories that leave nature self-producing where possible (epigenesis over occasionalism/preformation)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the production of organised beings, favour explanations that make nature self-producing (epigenesis or generic preformation) rather than Occasionalism or hyperphysic that invoke continual supernatural interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant critiques Occasionalism as 'losing nature' and finds individual preformation (supernatural implants of each individual) implausible; he views epigenesis (nature produces organised beings via capacities supplied in original products) as methodologically preferable because it 'with the least expenditure of the supernatural leaves to nature all that follows after the first beginning.' This is a methodological preference, not a proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume an original organisation or formative impulse when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging organised beings, naturalists should assume an original organisation or formative impulse in organised matter that employs mechanical laws to produce and develop organised forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant endorses that the naturalist 'must ... lay down as basis an original organisation' which 'uses that very mechanism in order to produce fresh organised forms.' Blumenbach's distinction between a formative impulse in organised matter and the merely mechanical formative power of crude matter is cited as exemplary: treat organised matter as possessing an undeterminable but recognizable formative principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret hereditary variations teleologically when they enter generative power
rubrics_metrics.description: If a character change is hereditary and taken up into the generative power, judge such variation as an occasional development of purposive capacities originally present in the species (with a view to preservation), rather than as mere contingency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant argues that where variation is hereditary and incorporated into generative capacity, it should be seen as development of originally purposive capacities; otherwise we would lack certainty whether parts of a species' form are purposive or contingent. This assigns a teleological interpretive role to heredity in assessing purposiveness.
